source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Arkansas River (north) to Mexican settlements (south); Taos and Santa Fe (west) to Cross Timbers, Texas (east)
summary: The book gives the extent of Comancheria as claimed by the Comanche in 1836, bounded by the Arkansas River, the Mexican settlements, Taos/Santa Fe and the Cross Timbers. This is the pre-treaty homeland that later treaties shrank.
verbatim_quote: In 1836, the Comanche claimed all the land between the Arkansas River to the north, the Mexican settlements to the south, from present-day Taos and Santa Fe in New Mexico to the west, and Cross-Timbers
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Royce shows only treaty-defined areas (478, 510, 511); the earlier, much larger Comanche claim is not depicted.
map_implication: Add an 'asserted homeland c.1836' context layer for Comancheria, including the Arkansas River border in SE Colorado; label as approximate.
notes: Boundaries are descriptive only; no map or primary source cited.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Indian removal (1830s)
summary: The Comanche objected to the US removing eastern tribes into present-day Oklahoma because it was Comanche hunting ground. Land 'given' to removed nations was taken from Plains nations who were never asked.
verbatim_quote: The tribe strongly objected to other Indian tribes being removed to lands in present-day Oklahoma in the 1830s because it was part of their hunting grounds.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Royce treats removal-era Indian Territory grants as US land to give; Comanche/Kiowa prior use is not recorded.
map_implication: Flag western Indian Territory removal reserves as overlapping Comanche/Kiowa hunting grounds without their consent.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: San Antonio, Republic of Texas (Council House)
summary: Twelve Comanche leaders who came to San Antonio for peace talks in 1840 were killed by Texans during the talks. Republic of Texas President Lamar had favored a war of extermination.
verbatim_quote: Comanche leaders arrived in San Antonio for new peace negotiations in 1840, but 12 of these leaders were killed by Texans during the peace talks.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Pre-US-statehood Texas action; absent from federal treaty record.
map_implication: Add a point event at San Antonio 1840 (Council House Fight) in a violence layer; Republic of Texas actor.
notes: Book does not name it the Council House Fight; that identification is mine and widely documented.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Comanche treaty of 1846 (unnamed in book; likely Treaty of Council Springs, 1846-05-15)
summary: After more than a year of US effort, only one of many Comanche bands signed the 1846 treaty recognizing US jurisdiction. The treaty was then presented as a Comanche treaty.
verbatim_quote: only one of the many Comanche bands signed a treaty recognizing the jurisdiction of the United States
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Kappler lists a 'Treaty with the Comanche, etc., 1846' as a nation-level instrument.
map_implication: In the treaty record, note that only one Comanche band signed the 1846 treaty.
notes: Identification with Council Springs 1846 (9 Stat. 844) is my inference; verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
nations: Kiowa; Comanche; Osage; Wichita; Creek; Cherokee; Choctaw; Waco
place: Fort Gibson / Camp Holmes, present-day Oklahoma
instrument: Treaty of Camp Holmes, 1835-08-24
instrument_cite: 7 Stat. 474 (per atlas TLA-T-198; not cited in book)
summary: The Kiowa sent 15 chiefs to the 1834 Fort Gibson council but objected to the terms and left without signing anything. The 1835 treaty's shared-hunting-ground terms therefore did not bind the Kiowa.
verbatim_quote: The Kiowa objected to the treaty’s terms and left the council early without signing any agreements.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Camp Holmes is often described as a southern Plains peace treaty; Kiowa non-participation is easy to miss.
map_implication: Mark Camp Holmes 1835 as not signed by the Kiowa.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa, etc., 1837 (Fort Gibson)
summary: The US offered gifts and trade goods to get the Kiowa to sign; ten chiefs (including Sensondacat, Kehimi, Takatacouche) signed, but principal chief Dohasan never did. The treaty recognized Kiowa hunting rights on the southern plains.
verbatim_quote: offered gifts and trade goods to persuade them to sign a new treaty... Dohasan, the principal chief, never signed the treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Kappler presents the 1837 treaty as a Kiowa national act; the principal chief's absence is not noted.
map_implication: Note principal chief did not sign 1837 Kiowa treaty; record recognized Kiowa hunting rights on the southern plains.
notes: Quote joins two sentences from p.38 with an ellipsis.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
nations: Kiowa; Comanche; Kiowa Apache; Cheyenne; Arapaho
place: Arkansas River, present-day Kansas (and SE Colorado)
instrument: Great Peace of 1840 (intertribal)
summary: In 1840 the Kiowa and Cheyenne ended their war, agreed to share hunting grounds and recognized the Arkansas River as the border between them. This intertribal agreement fixes a Native-made boundary on the Arkansas.
verbatim_quote: They agreed to share hunting grounds and recognized the Arkansas River in present-day Kansas as the border between the tribes.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats Arkansas River lands only via US treaties (Fort Laramie 1851, Fort Wise 1861, Little Arkansas 1865).
map_implication: Show the Arkansas River as an 1840 intertribal boundary (Kiowa-Comanche south, Cheyenne-Arapaho north), relevant to SE Colorado.
notes: Book says 'present-day Kansas'; the river also runs through SE Colorado.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Fort Atkinson (book says present-day Kansas on p.31, but 'near present-day Davis, Oklahoma' on p.39)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27
instrument_cite: 10 Stat. 1013; Kappler II p.600 (per atlas seed TLA-T-262, not cited in book)
summary: The Kiowa were reluctant; band chief Setangya (Sitting Bear) signed for the tribe while principal chief Dohasan and other leaders disagreed. Raids continued, suggesting the treaty lacked broad consent.
verbatim_quote: The Kiowa were reluctant to sign, but the band chief, Setangya (Sitting Bear), signed for the tribe. Dohasan and other leaders disagreed with the treaty
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Kappler records the treaty as made with the Kiowa nation; principal chief's dissent not shown.
map_implication: Annotate Fort Atkinson 1853 as signed for the Kiowa by a band chief over the principal chief's objection.
notes: Location conflict inside the book: Fort Atkinson was on the Arkansas near present Dodge City, Kansas; 'Davis, Oklahoma' on p.39 looks like an error ; verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Santa Fe Trail; territory south of the Arkansas River
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27, Article 3
instrument_cite: 10 Stat. 1013; Kappler II p.600 (per atlas seed TLA-T-262, not cited in book)
summary: Article 3 granted the US the right to lay out roads, posts and 'reservations of land necessary thereto'. The book says the nations understood a wagon-wheel-width road, but trails grew up to two miles wide, destroying timber and game, and the 1858 Colorado gold rush made the treaty unenforceable.
verbatim_quote: The Indian Nations understood they were consenting to a road or highway no wider than the width of a wagon-wheel track. Instead, the road was sometimes up to two miles wide
sources_cited_by_source: None for this commentary (author's comment)
federal_account_contrast: Federal text reads as a general right-of-way grant; Native understanding was far narrower.
map_implication: Add Santa Fe Trail corridor note: right-of-way consent understood as narrow track; damage beyond consent.
notes: Author openly labels comments 'biased criticisms and witticisms' (p.46).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27, preamble and Article 4
instrument_cite: 10 Stat. 1013; Kappler II p.600 (per atlas seed TLA-T-262, not cited in book)
summary: The treaty itself describes the nations as 'inhabiting the said territory south of the Arkansas River' and repeatedly refers to 'their said territories', an implicit US acknowledgment of their territory. No land was ceded.
verbatim_quote: the Camanche [sic], and Kiowa, and Apache tribes or nations of Indians, inhabiting the said territory south of the Arkansas River.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text reproduced
federal_account_contrast: Royce lists no cession for 1853; the recognition of territory is not drawn.
map_implication: Draw 1853 Fort Atkinson 'territories inhabited' (south of Arkansas River) as recognized occupancy, not a cession; includes SE Colorado south of the Arkansas.
notes: No boundaries beyond 'south of the Arkansas River'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27, Articles 6, 7, 9, 10
instrument_cite: 10 Stat. 1013; Kappler II p.600 (per atlas seed TLA-T-262, not cited in book)
summary: Article 6 promised $18,000 a year for ten years (plus five more at the President's discretion) in goods; Article 7 promised US protection and compensation for depredations by US citizens. The author found no compensation for treaty violations in the annual Indian appropriations acts of those years.
verbatim_quote: I could not find any evidence in the annual Indian Appropriations Acts during these years where there was compensation for losses from treaty violations.
sources_cited_by_source: Author's review of annual Indian Appropriations Acts (not individually cited)
federal_account_contrast: Federal record shows the promise; non-performance of Article 7 is not catalogued.
map_implication: Record Fort Atkinson Art.7 protection/compensation promise as unperformed (per PSL); Art.6 delivery to be verified.
notes: Book does not say whether the $18,000 annuities themselves were delivered. Art.6 commentary calls 'by these presents' a bribe; that is a misreading of a standard legal phrase and should not be repeated as evidence.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27, Article 8
instrument_cite: 10 Stat. 1013; Kappler II p.600 (per atlas seed TLA-T-262, not cited in book)
summary: Article 8 let the US withhold all or part of the annuities from a whole tribe until offenders were surrendered, i.e. collective punishment through food and goods. Later the US threatened to end treaty payments when Kiowa defended their land (p.40).
verbatim_quote: then the United States may withhold the whole part or a part of the annuities mentioned in the sixth article of this treaty, from the tribe so offending
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text reproduced
federal_account_contrast: Treated in the federal record as a routine enforcement clause.
map_implication: Tag annuity-withholding clauses as a structural coercion lever.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27; Fort Laramie Treaty 1851
summary: The author suggests that, as at Fort Laramie 1851, Fitzpatrick likely picked the 'chiefs and headmen' rather than letting bands select them, noting he forced the Lakota to name one leader over 22 tiyospayes.
verbatim_quote: we could assume that the “chiefs and leaders” were not selected by their bands but followed the practice perfected by Thomas Fitzpatrick during the negotiations of the Fort Laramie Treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: None
federal_account_contrast: Federal text says signers were chiefs and headmen of the nations.
map_implication: Do not flag Fort Atkinson as illegitimate on this basis alone; record as an inference.
notes: Explicitly an assumption by analogy; no Fort Atkinson evidence offered.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Pike's Peak region, Colorado; Kiowa territory
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche, Kiowa, and Apache, Fort Atkinson, 1853-07-27 (violated)
summary: The 1858 Pike's Peak gold rush sent thousands through Kiowa land and settlements were built illegally; the US did not stop these violations but threatened to cut treaty payments and send troops when the Kiowa resisted.
verbatim_quote: Settlements were quickly being built illegally on tribal lands, and the United States did not attempt to stop treaty violations made by the Euro-Americans.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Federal record dates loss of these lands to later treaties, not to earlier unauthorized occupation.
map_implication: Mark settler occupation of Colorado lands south of the Arkansas as preceding any Kiowa/Comanche cession.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Sand Creek, near Fort Lyon, Colorado Territory
summary: Governor John Evans began a policy of extermination; about 500 Cheyenne and Arapaho camped under promised protection with a US flag were attacked by Chivington's Colorado militia, killing more than 130, mostly women and children. The book says news of it convinced Plains nations the US could not be trusted, shaping 1865 and 1867 talks.
verbatim_quote: More than 130 Indians were killed, primarily women and children. News of the Sand Creek Massacre spread across the plains, proving that the United States could not be trusted.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Atlas already covers Sand Creek; book links it to Kiowa/Comanche treaty context.
map_implication: Link Sand Creek to Little Arkansas 1865 and Medicine Lodge 1867 as context for consent under threat.
notes: Kiowa-chapter mention; covered in depth elsewhere in the book.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
summary: Kit Carson's troops attacked Kiowa and Comanche winter camps; one camp of 176 tipis was burned with all food and supplies, leaving many without shelter or food. Carson was a US commissioner at Little Arkansas less than a year later.
verbatim_quote: A total of 176 tipis were destroyed, along with all food and supplies. Many people were left without shelter, clothing, or food that winter.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Treaty text lists Kit Carson as a commissioner with no reference to his attack.
map_implication: Add a point event (likely First Battle of Adobe Walls, Nov 1864) and note Carson's role as 1865 treaty commissioner.
notes: Book says 'around 1864' and does not name Adobe Walls; identification is mine.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Council ground on the Little Arkansas River, eight miles from its mouth, near present Wichita, Kansas
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18, preamble and Article 6
instrument_cite: Book endnote 4 (text reproduced); Stat./Kappler cite not given in book
summary: Some Comanche bands were absent; Article 6 made the signers promise to bring in absentees, whose mere receipt of annuities would bind them. The preamble nonetheless declares signers 'duly authorized', and the book comments that many leaders of both nations did not sign.
verbatim_quote: made binding on all parties whenever such absentees shall have participated in the beneficial provisions of this treaty. Comment: Many of the two Nations’ leaders did not sign this treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text reproduced (endnote 4); Kansapedia for p.31
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats the treaty as binding both nations from signing.
map_implication: Flag 1865 cession as signed without several Comanche bands; consent of absentees was deemed from accepting goods.
notes: Contradiction: p.41 says 'all the leading chiefs eventually signed it'; p.54 says many leaders did not sign. Royce areas from atlas crosswalk.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: NE corner of New Mexico; SE corner of New Mexico; Red River at mouth of North Fork; 98th meridian; Cimarron River; southern boundary of Kansas
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18, Article 2
instrument_cite: Book endnote 4 (text reproduced); Stat./Kappler cite not given in book
summary: Article 2 set apart a reservation 'for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation' of the tribes, bounded from the NE corner of New Mexico south to its SE corner, NE to the Red River opposite the North Fork mouth, down the Red to the 98th meridian, north to the Cimarron, up it to the Kansas line, west along Kansas to its SW corner, then west to the start. The book says it held over 39 million acres; within two years it was cut back at Medicine Lodge.
verbatim_quote: shall be and is hereby set apart for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation of the tribes who are parties to this treaty
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text reproduced
federal_account_contrast: Royce 478/511 shows it as a reservation; the federal record rarely marks it as a guarantee broken within two years.
map_implication: Draw the 1865 Little Arkansas reservation exactly from Art.2 calls (includes Texas panhandle and Oklahoma panhandle) as 'promised 1865, taken 1867'.
notes: Clause 'or such portion... as may hereafter... be designated by the President' made the guarantee conditional; the author calls the vagueness unacceptable. Most of the area lay in Texas, which held its public lands, so the US could not deliver it (my note; not in book).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Country north of the Cimarron River and west of the eastern boundary of New Mexico (includes SE Colorado and SW Kansas)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18, Article 2 relinquishment clause
instrument_cite: Book endnote 4 (text reproduced); Stat./Kappler cite not given in book
summary: Article 2 had the signers relinquish all claims outside the reservation, 'more especially' north of the Cimarron and west of New Mexico's eastern boundary. This is the clause that extinguished Kiowa and Comanche claims in southeastern Colorado, signed while some Comanche bands were absent.
verbatim_quote: relinquish all claims or rights in and to any portion of the United States or territories, except such as is embraced within the limits aforesaid
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text reproduced
federal_account_contrast: Royce draws this as a cession; the book frames the whole article as 'suspect'.
map_implication: For Colorado polygons ceded by Kiowa/Comanche in 1865, add caveat: absent bands, Article 2 judged suspect, reservation promised in return was cut two years later.
notes: Clause text literally reads 'north of the Cimarone River and west of the eastern boundary of New Mexico'; the Royce cession number for this relinquishment should be checked.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Unsettled country south of the Arkansas River
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18, Article 3
instrument_cite: Book endnote 4 (text reproduced); Stat./Kappler cite not given in book
summary: Until removal, the tribes were 'expressly permitted to reside upon and range at pleasure' over unsettled land south of the Arkansas that they claimed as originally theirs. This is a US admission of their original claim south of the Arkansas, including Colorado.
verbatim_quote: expressly permitted to reside upon and range at pleasure throughout the unsettled portions of that part of the country they claim as originally theirs, which lies south of the Arkansas River
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text reproduced
federal_account_contrast: Interim occupancy right is not shown in Royce.
map_implication: Add 1865 interim occupancy/hunting right south of the Arkansas River (incl. SE Colorado) as a reserved right.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
nations: Kiowa; Comanche; Kiowa Apache; Cheyenne; Arapaho
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18
summary: The Kansapedia-derived narrative says the tribes agreed to settle in western Kansas but Kansas lobbied against the treaty and they were forced elsewhere; it also says Dohasan protested but all leading chiefs eventually signed.
verbatim_quote: The tribes agreed to settle in western Kansas. The State of Kansas lobbied against the Treaty, and tribes were forced to settle elsewhere.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Treaty text (p.51) places the Kiowa-Comanche reservation south of Kansas, not in western Kansas.
map_implication: Do not map a western Kansas reservation from this; needs verification. Kansas lobbying may relate to the Cheyenne-Arapaho 1865 treaty.
notes: Conflicts with Art.2 boundary and with p.31 ('agreed to live in Indian Territory').

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Comanche and Kiowa, Little Arkansas River, 1865-10-18, Articles 4 and 5
instrument_cite: Book endnote 4 (text reproduced); Stat./Kappler cite not given in book
summary: Article 4 promised compensation for injury from roads and posts; Article 5 promised $10 per capita (rising to $15 after removal) annually for 40 years, on a base of 4,000 people. The author found little or no evidence of compensation and notes the treaty lasted only about two years before replacement.
verbatim_quote: There is little or no evidence that an invader was ever charged with violating this treaty or that anyone among the Tribes received compensation.
sources_cited_by_source: None
federal_account_contrast: 40-year annuity was superseded by Medicine Lodge; federal record does not net what was owed vs paid.
map_implication: Record 1865 40-year per-capita promise and its early supersession; check payments in appropriations acts.
notes: Author also says the treaty had 'scarcely been ratified for a few weeks' before a new standard; ratification date not given in book.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Act of March 29, 1867 (sec. 6 repealing treaty-making authority); Act of July 20, 1867 (Peace Commission); N.G. Taylor report of July 12, 1867
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 7 (book); Cong. Globe 451-452, 507, 623-624, 655; ICC Docket 257 (Aug 9, 1971)
summary: Quoting ICC Docket 257, the book shows Congress repealed treaty-making authority in March 1867, then Commissioner Taylor urged its repeal and a large removal territory south of Kansas including the Texas staked plains. The book reads this as proof the Peace Commission was designed for removal, not negotiation.
verbatim_quote: recommend that a large territory be set apart south of the southern line of Kansas and west of Arkansas, including the present Indian Territory and the country known as the staked plains of Texas
sources_cited_by_source: ICC Docket 257, Opinion on Motion for Summary Judgment of Recognized Title, Aug 9, 1971; Kuykendall dissent pp.123-131; Congressional Globe (endnotes 5-11)
federal_account_contrast: Federal narrative frames Medicine Lodge as a peace negotiation; this shows a predetermined removal plan.
map_implication: Link Medicine Lodge to the 1867 removal policy; cite ICC Docket 257.
notes: Book's 'conspired to illegally construct a plan' is the author's conclusion. Book is unclear whether quoted material is from majority or Kuykendall dissent.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: ICC Docket 257, Kiowa, Comanche and Apache Tribes v. United States
instrument_cite: ICC Docket 257 (Aug 9, 1971)
summary: The ICC heard a KCA motion for summary judgment of recognized title; the book says there were favorable findings for the tribes, opposed by Chairman Kuykendall in dissent, followed by an appeal to the Court of Claims.
verbatim_quote: This information is taken directly from Commissioner Jerome K. Kuykendall, Chairman of the Indian Claims Commission, dissent pp. 123-131, to have the favorable findings on behalf of the Tribes dismissed.
sources_cited_by_source: ICC Docket 257
federal_account_contrast: Shows ICC split on recognized title for KCA lands.
map_implication: Add ICC Docket 257 to KCA polygons; details promised later in the book.
notes: Book says 'U.S. Claims Commission Court', presumably the US Court of Claims. Outcome not in this chunk.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
nations: Kiowa; Comanche; Kiowa Apache; Cheyenne; Arapaho
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 581; Kappler II pp.977-982 (per atlas seed TLA-T-364; book endnote 15 reproduces text)
summary: The book states the tribes were coerced by threats of starvation and military intimidation into accepting a shared reservation between the Canadian and Red Rivers and allowing railroads.
verbatim_quote: The tribes were forcibly coerced to agree by threats of starvation and military intimidation to share a reservation between the Canadian and Red Rivers in present-day southwestern Oklahoma.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Kappler/NARA present Medicine Lodge as a negotiated peace treaty.
map_implication: Flag Royce 510/511 (1867 Kiowa-Comanche cession) as signed under duress (starvation and military threat).
notes: No specific threat is documented in this chunk; Sand Creek (1864) and Carson's 1864 raid provide context.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 581; Kappler II pp.977-982 (per atlas seed TLA-T-364; book endnote 15 reproduces text)
summary: Gui-pago (Lone Wolf) was the only Kiowa leader who did not sign Medicine Lodge. With Dohasan dead (1866), Kiowa leadership was divided between Kicking Bird (peace) and Lone Wolf and Satanta (resistance).
verbatim_quote: Gui-pago was the only Kiowa leader who did not sign the Medicine Lodge Treaty.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Federal text says signers were 'duly authorized and empowered to act for the body of the people'.
map_implication: Note Lone Wolf (the elder) did not sign Medicine Lodge.
notes: Do not confuse with Lone Wolf the younger of Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock (1903).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Washita River at 98th meridian; 30 river-miles west of Fort Cobb; North Fork of Red River / 100th meridian; main Red River
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21, Article 2
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 581; Kappler II pp.977-982 (per atlas seed TLA-T-364; book endnote 15 reproduces text)
summary: Article 2 set apart a reservation from where the Washita crosses the 98th meridian, up the Washita to 30 river-miles west of Fort Cobb, due west to the North Fork of the Red (or to the 100th meridian then south to it), down the North Fork to the Red, down the Red to the 98th meridian, then north to the start. The US 'solemnly' promised no one unauthorized would ever pass over, settle or reside there.
verbatim_quote: the United States now solemnly agrees that no persons except those herein authorized so to do... shall ever be permitted to pass over, settle upon, or reside in the territory described in this article
sources_cited_by_source: Treaty text reproduced (endnote 15)
federal_account_contrast: The 'ever' guarantee was broken by the Jerome Agreement/1900 Act (outside this chunk).
map_implication: Draw the 1867 KCA reservation from Art.2 calls as 'guaranteed forever 1867'; link to 1892/1900 taking.
notes: Narrative on p.41 describes it as between the Red, North Fork and Washita; and earlier as between Canadian and Red (the combined Medicine Lodge area incl. Cheyenne-Arapaho).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21, Article 2 pencil additions
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 581; Kappler II pp.977-982 (per atlas seed TLA-T-364; book endnote 15 reproduces text)
summary: A Department of State note says words in brackets were written in pencil in the original, the rest in ink; the pencil additions include the boundary lead-in and the phrase 'with the consent of the United States' limiting whom the tribes could admit. The author says leaders rejected the boundaries and location, yet they were inserted in a pre-drafted document.
verbatim_quote: The leaders of Kiowa and Comanche rejected these boundaries and the location, yet they were inserted in the document. This is a perfect example of a document that had been previously constructed
sources_cited_by_source: Department of State note on original treaty; Peace Commission proceedings
federal_account_contrast: Ratified text shows no indication the boundaries were disputed or that consent language was added in pencil.
map_implication: Flag Medicine Lodge Art.2 text as containing pencil insertions of unknown timing; check NARA original.
notes: Book does not say who wrote the pencil words or when; do not call it forgery without archival check. Pencil markers appear in the text as '[addition in pencil*]' and '[phrase addition A underlined made in pencil*]'.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21
instrument_cite: Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission of 1867-68 (endnotes 12-14)
summary: Ten Bear (Comanche) said the proposed land was too small and that Texans had taken the best country; Satanta (Kiowa) said he did not want to settle on a reservation. The book argues the commissioners ignored what the leaders said and the result was preordained.
verbatim_quote: that which you now say we must live on is too small. The Texans have taken away the places where the grass grew the thickest and the timber was the best.
sources_cited_by_source: Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission of 1867-68
federal_account_contrast: Treaty text records assent; recorded speeches show refusal of the land offered.
map_implication: Attach Ten Bear and Satanta statements to the Medicine Lodge record as stated objection to the reservation.
notes: Satanta refers to a reservation 'near the Mountains' (Wichita Mountains).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Medicine Lodge Creek, Kansas; Red River and Wichita Mountains
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21 (hunting concession)
instrument_cite: Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission (endnote 14)
summary: Senator Henderson told the council the Kiowa and Comanche could hunt 'up the river' while warning that the buffalo would vanish, a remark the transcript records with laughter. The narrative calls the hunting right a last-minute concession over former lands in Kansas (p.31) or Kansas and Texas (p.41).
verbatim_quote: When that day comes, the Indian must leave his father’s road, or suffer and probably die.(Laughter.)
sources_cited_by_source: Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission (endnote 14)
federal_account_contrast: Hunting right appears in the treaty (Art.11, not in this chunk) as a neutral clause; the transcript shows the US expected it to lapse with the buffalo.
map_implication: Map the off-reservation hunting right south of the Arkansas as reserved; note US expectation of its extinction.
notes: Inconsistency: p.31 says Kansas; p.41 says Kansas and Texas.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, Medicine Lodge Creek, 1867-10-21 (rations/annuities)
instrument_cite: 15 Stat. 581; Kappler II pp.977-982 (per atlas seed TLA-T-364; book endnote 15 reproduces text)
summary: After a failed hunt, the Kiowa asked the agent for promised provisions but got none because Congress had not yet acted on the treaty; by 1871 none of the promised rations had been delivered.
verbatim_quote: They requested provisions that were promised in the treaty from the Indian agent. Congress had yet to approve the treaty. Thus, no provisions were granted.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Atlas seed gives Medicine Lodge proclamation 1868-07-25; book indicates obligations went unmet in practice.
map_implication: Add Medicine Lodge non-delivery of rations 1868-1871 to violations catalog.
notes: 'None... by 1871' may overstate; verify against agency reports.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Washita River, Indian Territory (Black Kettle's camp)
summary: Custer's troops attacked Black Kettle's sleeping Cheyenne camp on the Washita, killing 103 including Black Kettle and his wife and taking 53 women and children. The book calls Sheridan's campaign part of the 1867 Peace Commission policy, signaling resistance meant extermination.
verbatim_quote: One hundred and three Cheyenne, including Black Kettle and his wife, were killed, and 53 women and children were taken.
sources_cited_by_source: Endnote 2 (Kansapedia)
federal_account_contrast: Army record called it a battle; occurred within a year of Medicine Lodge.
map_implication: Add Washita 1868 as massacre and hostage-taking event linked to Medicine Lodge.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
summary: Lone Wolf and Satanta were seized while traveling under a white flag to tell Custer the Kiowa were not at the Washita; the US threatened to execute them unless the Kiowa gathered at Fort Cobb, and the tribe complied.
verbatim_quote: The United States threatened to execute the chiefs unless the Kiowa gathered at Fort Cobb. The tribe quickly complied
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Concentration on the reservation is usually presented as compliance with Medicine Lodge, not as result of hostage-taking.
map_implication: Tag Kiowa removal onto the 1867 reservation as achieved by hostage-taking of leaders.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
summary: Sherman ordered Satanta, Setangya and Big Tree arrested and sent to Texas for trial; Setangya was killed en route; the others were sentenced to hang, commuted to life with forced railroad labor, released 1873; Satanta was re-imprisoned in 1874 and died by suicide.
verbatim_quote: The three leaders were seized, handcuffed, and transported by armed guards to Texas.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Shows a state court prosecuting treaty-nation leaders for acts of war.
map_implication: Add imprisonment of Kiowa treaty signers by Texas to the violence/state-action layer.
notes: Includes Setangya's Koitsenko death song (p.42).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: Quaker (Peace) Policy, 1869
summary: Agent Lawrie Tatum withheld rations to force cultural change; later the government lowered rations to starvation levels to press assimilation while settlers pushed to open the reservation.
verbatim_quote: The government increased the pressure on the Kiowa to assimilate, lowering food rations to levels that caused starvation.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
federal_account_contrast: Ration policy is not in treaty records; shows starvation used as a policy tool on a treaty reservation.
map_implication: Add 'sign or starve' context to later KCA land loss (Jerome Agreement era).

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Texas panhandle (Palo Duro Canyon, unnamed in book)
summary: Mackenzie's troops destroyed a Kiowa, Comanche and Cheyenne village, its food, shelter and horses, forcing the people back to Fort Sill; all surrendered by April 1875.
verbatim_quote: All the food, clothing, supplies, and shelter were destroyed, and the horses were slaughtered.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
map_implication: Add Palo Duro 1874 event; book writes 'Ronald Mackenzie' (actually Ranald S. Mackenzie).
notes: Identification as Palo Duro is mine.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
summary: After Texas Rangers killed a Kiowa in 1879, the book says Congress made it illegal for any Kiowa to leave the reservation; in the 1880s ranchers illegally used tribal land; the Kiowa refused leasing though some Comanche leased.
verbatim_quote: Some ranchers illegally used tribal land, and others tried to lease it. The Kiowa continually refused to lease any of their land
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
map_implication: Note illegal grazing and Kiowa/Comanche split over leasing on the 1867 reservation.
notes: The claim that 'Congress' barred Kiowa from leaving is unsourced and probably an administrative order; verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
place: Kiowa reservation and off-reservation boarding schools
summary: Kiowa children were forced or captured into boarding schools that banned language and religion; three beaten boys froze to death after escaping in 1891 and a 1892 measles outbreak killed more than 220 children. Agent E.E. White banned the Sun Dance in 1888.
verbatim_quote: Some children were captured and placed in boarding schools far from the reservation.
sources_cited_by_source: Book says pp.29-45 history was copied from Kansapedia (Kansas Historical Society), endnotes 1-3
map_implication: Add boarding school harms to KCA record; Sun Dance ban 1888.
notes: 'More than 220 children' figure unsourced; verify.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
instrument: KCA treaties generally
summary: The author asserts that Indian agents produced compliant signers who bound whole nations, and that some government interpreters maliciously distorted treaty contents to benefit themselves.
verbatim_quote: In many cases, the Indian agents produced Indians who were compliant and agreeable to every demand of those agents and became the signers.
sources_cited_by_source: None
federal_account_contrast: Federal texts recite signers as duly authorized.
map_implication: Use only as framing; requires instrument-specific evidence before flagging.
notes: General claim; no specific interpreter named in this chunk.

source_doc: PSL TREC 2024 (The Legal and Political History of Colorado Tribes)
summary: Source caveat: the book states that most of the Comanche and Kiowa history before Part 2 (pp.29-45) was copied directly from Kansapedia with permission, so those pages are a secondary encyclopedia source, not Native-authored analysis. notes: Affects evidence level of all p.29-45 findings.
